title: The Wesley Brothers — Parallel Lives
subtitle: A timeline of moments, movements, and the works born from them
note: The unique feature of this data: John and Charles were responding to the same events, the same scriptures, the same crises — one in prose sermons, one in verse. This parallel is the soul of the Wesley Explorer.

moments.event: John Wesley born
moments.description: Fifteenth child of Samuel and Susanna Wesley. Susanna's methodical approach to raising her children — each given dedicated one-on-one time, each taught Scripture from infancy — would mark both brothers permanently.

moments.event: Charles Wesley born
moments.description: Born premature, so sickly his parents feared he would not live. The fourth surviving son. His mother Susanna noted he seemed to exist in a kind of silence — he did not cry like other infants — which she interpreted as peace.

moments.event: The Epworth Rectory Fire
moments.description: The rectory burns. Six-year-old John is rescued from a second-floor window moments before the roof collapses, the last family member saved. Samuel Wesley calls him 'a brand plucked from the burning' (Zech 3:2). John carries this self-understanding his entire life — he is preserved for a purpose.

john.impact: Formative identity: 'a brand plucked from the burning'

moments.event: John enters Christ Church, Oxford
moments.description: John goes up to Oxford. Charles follows in 1726. Both are formed by Oxford's rigorous classical education and its expectation of clerical discipline.

moments.event: The Holy Club founded
moments.description: Charles begins gathering a small group of students at Oxford for methodical Bible study, prayer, and charitable works — visiting prisoners, caring for the sick. When John returns from Epworth, he assumes leadership. Critics mock them: 'Methodists.' The brothers embrace the label.

john.role: Leader, organizer, theologian of the group

charles.role: Initiator, pastoral heart of the club

moments.later_significance: The Holy Club is the seed of global Methodism

moments.event: John preaches 'The Circumcision of the Heart' at Oxford
moments.description: John's earliest sermon in the 44 Standard Sermons. He already understands what inward holiness requires. But he has not yet experienced it. The sermon is prescient — he knows the destination before he knows the way.
moments.irony: John preaches entire sanctification 5 years before his conversion

moments.event: Georgia Mission
moments.description: Both brothers sail to Georgia, America, as missionaries to colonists and Native Americans. It is a systematic failure. John's rigid rule-based religion alienates the colonists. Charles serves as secretary to Governor Oglethorpe and has a miserable year before returning in 1736. John returns in 1738, writing in his journal: 'I went to America to convert the Indians; but oh! who shall convert me?' On the voyage they meet Moravian missionaries whose unshakeable peace in a storm haunts both brothers.

john.impact: Failure strips him of confidence in his own religion

moments.john_journal_quote: I went to America to convert the Indians; but oh! who shall convert me?

moments.event: ALDERSGATE — Both brothers transformed within three days
moments.description: Charles, ill and staying at the home of a Mr. Bray, reads Luther's commentary on Galatians and on Whitsunday, May 21, experiences what he calls a conversion — the trust that Christ died for him, not mankind abstractly. Three days later, John attends a Moravian meeting in Aldersgate Street where someone reads Luther's preface to Romans, and he famously writes: 'I felt my heart strangely warmed.' Charles writes 'Where Shall My Wondering Soul Begin' that night — his first published hymn. Both brothers use the same image: chains broken, prison doors opened.

john.journal_quote: I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that He had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death.

charles.note: Charles's Aldersgate was May 21 — 3 days before John's

moments.shared_imagery: Both independently wrote about chains falling off and prison doors opening

parallel_works.john: Sermon 1: Salvation by Faith (published same year)
parallel_works.charles: CW018: Where Shall My Wondering Soul Begin (written that night) + CW005: And Can It Be (written days later)

moments.event: Open-air preaching begins / First hymn collection published
moments.description: George Whitefield, excluded from Bristol churches, begins preaching in the open air to coal miners at Kingswood. He persuades John to do the same. John overcomes his scruples ('I thought the saving of souls almost a sin if it had not been done in a church') and begins preaching in fields. Charles publishes the first Methodist hymn collection: 'Hymns and Sacred Poems.' The movement has begun.

john.impact: Crosses the line into field preaching — now a movement, not a club

charles.impact: Publishes the movement's hymnbook — gives it a singing voice

parallel_works.charles: Hymns and Sacred Poems — sung proclamation

moments.event: Break with Whitefield over predestination
moments.description: George Whitefield and the Wesley brothers split over Calvinist predestination. Whitefield holds to double predestination; the Wesleys insist on universal atonement and free grace. Charles writes 'Come, Sinners, to the Gospel Feast' as a direct theological response — the invitation is genuinely for all. The breach is painful; all three men loved each other. It permanently defines two streams of evangelical Protestantism.

john.note: Publishes 'Free Grace' sermon directly against predestination

charles.note: CW015 ('Come Sinners to the Gospel Feast') encodes the universal invitation

moments.lasting_consequence: Calvinist vs. Wesleyan-Arminian divide in evangelical Protestantism

moments.event: Methodist societies spreading across England
moments.description: Class meetings, bands, and circuits multiply. Both brothers preach constantly, often in the face of violent mobs. Charles is arrested, stoned, and threatened repeatedly — yet continues. John organizes; Charles energizes. The movement has structure and song.

john.note: Preaches Scriptural Christianity at Oxford — his farewell to institutional religion

charles.note: Soldiers of Christ, Arise — the movement's battle hymn

moments.event: Hymns on the Lord's Supper published — Charles's theological masterwork
moments.description: Charles publishes 166 hymns on the Lord's Supper — his deepest, most sustained theological poetry. Together with Daniel Brevint's treatise on the Christian sacrament, it argues for a high view of eucharistic presence without transubstantiation. These are among the finest eucharistic hymns in any Christian tradition. John supports the project; the Supper as means of grace is central to both brothers' spirituality.

john.note: The Means of Grace — identical emphasis on the Supper as real channel of grace

charles.note: 166 hymns on Communion — the theological summit of Charles's career

parallel_works.charles: Hymns on the Lord's Supper (166 poems)

moments.event: Entire sanctification — the doctrine defined in sermon and song simultaneously
moments.description: John publishes 'Christian Perfection' (Sermon 40) and 'A Plain Account of Christian Perfection.' Charles writes 'Love Divine, All Loves Excelling.' Same doctrine, same year — one in analytical prose, one in lyric. The doctrine of perfect love — freedom from deliberate sin, pure motivation, complete love for God and neighbor — is the distinctive Wesleyan contribution to Christian theology.

john.note: Defines entire sanctification with theological precision

charles.note: Love Divine encodes the doctrine in unforgettable verse

parallel_works.charles: CW004: Love Divine, All Loves Excelling

moments.doctrine_note: The final stanza of Love Divine ('Finish then thy new creation') is the poetic summary of Wesley's entire sanctification doctrine

moments.event: Charles marries Sarah Gwynne — the brothers diverge
moments.description: Charles marries Sarah Gwynne on April 8. John disapproves initially — fears the movement will lose Charles's itinerant preaching. He is right. Charles gradually settles into domestic and local ministry. The two brothers remain in deep affection but their paths diverge. Charles still writes hymns; John still organizes circuits. But the years of side-by-side preaching are ending. Charles writes 'Forth in Thy Name, O Lord, I Go' — a theology of vocation for the person whose ministry is ordinary life.

john.note: Continues itinerant preaching until his death — 250,000 miles on horseback

charles.note: Forth in Thy Name — vocation theology as Charles settles into domestic life

moments.irony: Charles's hymn about consecrated ordinary work written as he stopped extraordinary itinerant work

moments.event: Lo, He Comes with Clouds Descending — eschatology in verse
moments.description: Charles publishes a revised version of John Cennick's eschatological hymn, producing 'Lo, He Comes with Clouds Descending.' Meanwhile John preaches 'The Great Assize.' Both brothers think about the end together — the final reckoning, the return of Christ, the divine court that supersedes all human courts.

parallel_works.charles: CW013: Lo, He Comes with Clouds Descending

moments.event: Short Hymns on Select Passages — Charles's most prolific year
moments.description: Charles publishes 'Short Hymns on Select Passages of Holy Scripture' — 2,030 hymns on Scripture passages, one of the most sustained acts of biblical meditation in Christian history. 'O Thou Who Camest from Above' (on Lev 6:13) and 'A Charge to Keep I Have' (on Lev 8:35) come from this collection. Charles is now 55 and settled in Bristol — he turns inward, meditating on Scripture verse by verse.

john.note: Wandering Thoughts — also becoming more inward and psychological

charles.note: 2030 hymns on Scripture — one hymn per passage, verse by verse through the Bible

moments.staggering_fact: 2,030 hymns in one publication — approximately one hymn for every passage Charles meditated on

moments.event: The Scripture Way of Salvation — Wesley's mature synthesis
moments.description: John publishes Sermon 43: 'The Scripture Way of Salvation.' Often called his greatest single sermon. Written at 62, it distills a lifetime of preaching and theological refinement. Salvation from its beginning in prevenient grace through justification to entire sanctification — all held together in a clear, balanced account. Charles the same year writes 'O Thou Who Camest from Above' — same arc, compressed into four stanzas.

john.note: The mature synthesis — everything he believed in one sermon

moments.event: Charles moves to London
moments.description: Charles moves his family from Bristol to Marylebone, London. He will spend his remaining years here — local ministry, music (his sons Charles Jr. and Samuel become accomplished musicians), and continued writing. John visits when his circuit brings him to London. The brothers are aging but still in close correspondence.

john.note: Still itinerant — will preach until weeks before his death

charles.note: London becomes his base; music fills his household

moments.event: Charles dies — John's last great grief
moments.description: Charles dies at his home in Marylebone on March 29, 1788. He dictates his final hymn, 'In Age and Feebleness Extreme,' to his wife Sarah. John, 84, preaches the funeral sermon. He cannot speak Charles's name without weeping. In his journal he writes simply: 'His least praise was his talent for poetry.' John lives three more years, preaching and organizing until the end.

john.note: Survives Charles by 3 years. Writes in journal: 'His least praise was his talent for poetry'

charles.last_hymn: CW052: In Age and Feebleness Extreme

moments.john_journal_on_charles: His least praise was his talent for poetry; although Dr. Watts did not scruple to say that that single poem, 'Wrestling Jacob,' was worth all the verses he himself had ever written.

moments.event: John Wesley dies
moments.description: John dies at his house in City Road, London. His last words: 'The best of all is, God is with us.' He had preached his last sermon eight days earlier. He left behind a movement of over 70,000 Methodists in Britain and 40,000 in America, hundreds of schools, the Kingswood School, the Arminian Magazine, and an organizational structure that would survive him for centuries. Between them, the brothers had changed the face of English-speaking Christianity.

john.last_words: The best of all is, God is with us
